# Hearts
Most living creatures have a heart. Some species, such as dionae and slimes, do not require one. A beating heart can still have a dangerous rhythm. Check the pulse and the patient's other injuries before treatment.
BPM means beats per minute. A standard human heart normally beats 80 times per minute. Different species have different resting rates and fibrillation thresholds.
For a normal human, anything more than 210 or less than 40 means that the heart is in fibrillations.
Fibrillations can be countered in many ways some are:
- if the heart is lacking BPM, then some hard drugs or using a defibrillator might work. - if the heart is beating more than it needs to, some relaxing drugs or a defibrillator might work.
Some medicines and drugs change the pulse. Epinephrine and omnizine stabilise it and can restart a stopped heart. Stimulants and sedatives can also push the pulse into a dangerous range; they are not interchangeable with a stabilising medicine.
## Defibrillator usage
The defibrillators found shiftstart in medical are [bold]MANUAL DEFIBRILLATORS[/bold] and they require proper use.
The ones that science can print and those found in paramedics lockers are called compact defibrillators (sometimes, an auto defibrillators or AEDs)
AEDs or compact defibrillators are easy in use, as they will try to change the BPM of the target by 45 closest to the standard BPM of the patient.
Manual defibrillators need to be properly used to not cause death to the patient.
# Manual Defibrillator Guide
M.E.D.s have 4 switches and one power flip, with a screen that tells the current heartrate of the patient. Interact with a nearby patient while the manual defibrillator is switched off to open its monitor without shocking them. The screen shows that patient's measured BPM, not a target setting. A shock also selects its recipient for monitoring. A reading of 0 can mean a stopped or missing heart; use the medical analyzer to distinguish them.
The flips and switches do the following:
- IO switch (power switch) - O is Off, I is ON. - Voltage flips - four identical switches. Only the number switched on matters; their positions do not select separate functions. Each enabled switch represents another 500V step. These steps change the pulse effect, not the battery cost or suffocation healing.
- 0 flips - The device cannot deliver a shock. - 1 flip/500V - Subtracts 80 BPM from a beating heart. Does not restart a stopped heart. - 2 flips/1000V - Subtracts 50 BPM from a beating heart. Does not restart a stopped heart. - 3 flips/1500V - Adds 150 BPM to a beating heart, or starts a stopped heart at 200 BPM. - 4 flips/2000V - Adds 200 BPM to a beating heart, or starts a stopped heart at 300 BPM.
For example, 250 BPM with two flips becomes 200 BPM; 30 BPM with three flips becomes 180 BPM. Repeating a raising setting keeps raising the pulse. One flip on a heart at 80 BPM can stop it, and four flips can create a dangerous rhythm.
A standard shock also treats 40 suffocation damage, but does not restore missing blood or replace breathing. A safe pulse alone does not mean that the patient has recovered. Continue treating their injuries and assisting their breathing when needed.
Stasis beds suppress the new circulation penalty from a missing or stopped heart while the patient is buckled in. This does not replace the missing heart or remove other injuries.
